items.prompt: Black to move. Black is thinking of g6. Pawns cannot go back, so this move changes which squares Black's pawns can guard. Tap the squares in Black's camp that become HOLES because of this move (squares no Black pawn can attack now or by advancing, which were not holes before).

claims.statement: Before the move the holes in Black's camp are a6 and c6.
After g6 the holes in Black's camp are a6, c6, f6 and h6.

hints: Which Black pawn guards f6 and h6 today? Ask what it can no longer reach once it has moved.
The e-pawn has left e7, and the f- and h-pawns stand beside the g-pawn on the 7th rank. Does any of them cover f6 or h6?
Two squares: one on the f-file and one on the h-file.
items.explain: Before g6 the pawn on g7 guards f6 and h6. After g6 no Black pawn can ever attack either square, so the holes are a6, c6, f6 and h6 and the new ones are f6 and h6. Whether an enemy piece can use them is a separate question.

items.prompt: Black to move. The g-pawn already stands on g6, so f6 and h6 are holes, and a White knight on e4 can reach f6. Tap the square where the bishop on f8 would cover both holes.

claims.statement: f6 and h6 are holes in Black's camp.
The bishop on f8 can go to e7, g7 or h6.
From g7 the bishop attacks both f6 and h6.
From e7 the bishop attacks f6 but not h6.

hints: Which squares must the bishop attack to take away both holes?
Check the three squares the bishop can reach: which one attacks f6 and h6 together?
It is the square the g-pawn just left.
items.explain: From g7 the bishop attacks f6 and h6, so a knight that lands on either square can be captured. From e7 the bishop covers f6 only.

items.prompt: White to move. f6 is a hole in Black's camp. Can the knight on e4 go to f6 and stand there without any Black piece being able to capture it? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: No Black pawn can ever attack f6.
The knight can go to f6.
No Black piece attacks f6.

hints: Who could capture a knight on f6? Look at pawns first, then at pieces.
Count the Black pieces that attack f6. The Black bishop stands on b7 behind its own knight.
Nothing attacks f6.
items.explain: f6 is a hole and no Black piece attacks it, so a knight on f6 cannot be captured at once. This checks only that the knight can stay; it does not claim that Nf6 is the best move.

items.prompt: White to move. f6 is a hole in Black's camp. Can the knight on e4 go to f6 and stand there without any Black piece being able to capture it? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: No Black pawn can ever attack f6.
Exactly one Black piece attacks f6.
The bishop on g7 attacks f6.

hints: This is the same hole. What differs from the first position? Count the Black pieces that attack f6.
Look at the bishop: which square is it on?
The bishop on g7 attacks f6.
items.explain: The hole is the same, but the bishop on g7 attacks f6, so a knight there can be captured. A bishop on the fianchetto square takes the hole away as a landing square.

items.prompt: White to move. Is f6 a hole in Black's camp? A hole is a square on Black's 3rd, 4th or 5th rank with no Black pawn on it that none of Black's pawns attacks now or can attack by advancing. Predict, then check.

claims.statement: f6 is not a hole in Black's camp.
A Black pawn attacks f6.
The Black pawn on e7 is the one that attacks f6.
a6, c6 and h6 are holes in Black's camp; f6 is not.

hints: Look at the Black pawns on the files beside f.
Is any of them low enough to attack f6?
The pawn on e7 attacks f6.
items.explain: The pawn on e7 still attacks f6, so f6 is not a hole. With the g-pawn on g6 only h6 is a hole (with a6 and c6 that already existed). Check which pawn still guards a square before you call it weak.

items.prompt: Black is about to push one kingside pawn one square. Which push creates a NEW square in Black's camp (on its 3rd to 5th rank) that no Black pawn can attack now or by advancing?

claims.statement: After g6 the holes are a6, c6, f6 and h6; f6 and h6 are new.
After h6 the holes are only a6 and c6, which already existed.
After f6 the holes are only a6 and c6, which already existed.

hints: Which pawn guards the squares in front of the king today? Ask what happens to its guard when it moves.
Only one of the three pawns is the sole guard of squares that no other pawn covers.
The pawn on the g-file.
items.explain: Only g6 gives up squares that no other Black pawn guards: f6 and h6. After h6 or f6 the squares in front of the king stay covered.

items.prompt: Black has already played g6 and is about to push one more pawn one square. Which push creates a NEW square in Black's camp (on its 3rd to 5th rank) that no Black pawn can attack now or by advancing?

claims.statement: Before the push the holes are a6, c6, f6 and h6.
After g5 the holes are a6, c6, f6, h5 and h6; h5 is new.
After h6 no new hole appears (h6 is now occupied).
After f6 no new hole appears (f6 is now occupied).

hints: Compare the holes before and after each push.
A push can fill a hole (a pawn standing on a square means it is not a hole) as well as make one.
The g-pawn moves again.
items.explain: Pushing the g-pawn on to g5 makes h5 a new hole. The h- and f-pushes only occupy squares that were already holes, so they add none.

items.prompt: White to move. Break with d5 now, or prepare first? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: d5 is at least 1.5 pawns worse than the best move (engine, depth 16).
After d5 two Black pieces (the pawn on c6 and the knight on b6) attack the pawn.
After d5 one White piece (the queen) defends it.

hints: Is the pawn break d5 available? Count the attackers and the defenders of d5 before you push.
The knight on b6 attacks d5 as well as the pawn on c6. What does that do to the count?
Play a developing or waiting move instead of the break.
items.explain: After d5 the pawn would be attacked twice (pawn c6, knight b6) and defended once (queen), and the engine rates d5 at least 1.5 pawns below the best quiet moves. Several quiet moves are about equal: the point is to prepare first and not break yet.

items.prompt: White is thinking of the quiet push d4-d5 (not a capture). After it, would the pawn on d5 attack a Black pawn on c6 or e6, offering an exchange? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: After d5 the pawn attacks only c6 and e6.
c6 is empty.
e6 is empty.

hints: A break offers an exchange. Which squares would the pawn on d5 attack?
Look at c6 and e6.
Both squares are empty, so there is nothing to exchange.
items.explain: The pawn on d4 already attacks c5 and e5, so the tension is on the board; pushing to d5 would give it up and would attack c6 and e6, which are empty. The push offers no exchange: it is an advance, not a break.

items.prompt: Black is thinking of the pawn move g5. Does that pawn attack a White pawn, offering an exchange? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: After g5 the pawn attacks only f4 and h4.
f4 is empty.
h4 is empty.

hints: A break offers an exchange. Which squares would the pawn on g5 attack?
Look at f4 and h4.
Both squares are empty, so there is nothing to exchange.
items.explain: A pawn on g5 would attack f4 and h4, and both squares are empty. The push offers no exchange, so it is an advance, not a break.

items.prompt: Black to move. Find a strong move.

claims.statement: No Black pawn attacks the pawn on d4.
Nh5 is the engine's best move (Stockfish 19 lite, depth 16).
The break e5 is at least 1.5 pawns worse than the best move (engine, depth 16).
After e5 four White pieces attack the pawn (rook e3, knight f3, pawn d4, bishop f4).
After e5 two Black pieces defend it.

hints: White's pawn on d4 is free. Is the break e5 ready? Count the attackers and the defenders of e5.
The White rook now stands on e3, in front of the e-file. What does that add to the count?
Do not break. A piece move that attacks the bishop on f4 is best.
items.explain: The pawn on d4 is free, but after e5 four White pieces would attack e5 and only two Black pieces defend it, and the engine rates e5 at least 1.5 pawns below Nh5. The rook on e3 is the only difference from the position where e5 was best.

feedback_by_move.e6e5: e5 is at least 150 centipawns worse than Nh5 here (engine, depth 16): the break square is attacked four times and defended twice.

items.prompt: Black to move. Is White's pawn on d4 a free centre pawn here: no Black pawn attacks it and it can advance? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: A Black pawn stands on e5.
One Black pawn, the pawn on e5, attacks d4.
No Black piece is loose.
No White piece is loose.

hints: Check the Black pawns near d4: does any of them attack it?
Look at e5.
The Black pawn on e5 already attacks the pawn on d4.
items.explain: A Black pawn on e5 already attacks the pawn on d4, so it is not free: the exchange is on the board and there is nothing to prepare. No piece hangs on either side, so the question is only about the pawn.

items.prompt: Black to move. Is White's pawn on d4 a free centre pawn here: no Black pawn attacks it and it can advance? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: No Black pawn attacks the pawn on d4.
A Black pawn stands on d5.
The pawn on d4 has no legal move.
No Black piece is loose.
No White piece is loose.
No tactic: the engine's best line wins at most a pawn.

hints: Free means two things: no enemy pawn attacks it, and it can advance. Check both.
Look at the square in front of the pawn.
A Black pawn on d5 blocks it, so the pawn cannot move.
items.explain: No Black pawn attacks d4, but the Black pawn on d5 blocks it, so the pawn has no move. It is not a free centre pawn that needs a break or a set-up.

claims.statement: The engine rates the position at least half a pawn in Black's favour (White's point of view, depth 16).
Both sides own the bishop pair.
No file is open or half-open for either side.
Black's pawns control b4 and d4 in White's half.
White's pawns control no square in Black's half.

hints: Fill the list first: pieces, pawns, files, space, king safety.
Both sides have the bishop pair. What else differs?
The engine prefers Black.
items.explain: The engine rates Black at least half a pawn better. Both sides own the bishop pair and no file is open, so those entries do not decide it. One checked difference: Black's pawns control b4 and d4, while White's pawns control no square in Black's half. That is a small space edge; the claims show the rating and this difference, not the full reason.

items.prompt: White to move. Does Black's pawn on e5 stand on a line of a White rook, bishop or queen: does any of those pieces attack it? Predict, then check.

items.explain: The pawn on e4 still blocks the rook, but two white men defend e4 and Nxe4 loses material: the engine rates it at least 3 pawns worse than its best move. The engine's top moves are the developing move Nc6 and the pawn move d5: here the obstruction is left alone.
